sections.title: IPv4 Addressing and the IPv4 Header

blocks.text:
The link layer delivers frames between devices attached to the same network segment. A request from a Spring Boot client to a server on another continent crosses dozens of such segments, owned by different organisations, built from different link technologies and using different frame formats. The network layer solves this problem. It defines a uniform packet format and a uniform address space that are independent of the underlying links, and it moves each packet hop by hop from the source host to the destination host. In the Internet this layer is implemented by the Internet Protocol (IP). Version 4 (IPv4, RFC 791) still carries the majority of traffic, and every other topic in this Part builds on its header and its addressing model.

IP is deliberately minimal. It is **connectionless**: each datagram is routed independently, and no state about a conversation is kept in the routers. It is **best effort**: a datagram can be lost, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order, and IP does not report these events to the sender except through the optional ICMP error messages described in a later chapter. Reliability, ordering and congestion control are the responsibility of the transport layer (TCP) or of the application. This division of labour keeps routers simple and fast, which is the main reason the design scaled.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The IPv4 address

An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number. It is written in dotted-decimal notation as four octets, each from 0 to 255, for example `192.168.1.10`, which is the binary value `11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010`. An address identifies a network **interface**, not a host. A router has one address per interface, and a multihomed server may have several.

Every address has two logical parts: a **network prefix** that identifies the network (subnet) and a **host part** that identifies the interface within it. Routers forward on the network prefix only. The boundary between the two parts is given by a subnet mask or a prefix length, described in the next chapter. Early IPv4 fixed the boundary by the value of the first bits (classes A, B and C with prefix lengths 8, 16 and 24). This classful scheme wasted address space and was replaced in 1993 by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR, RFC 4632). Class names survive only in vocabulary.

Every IP datagram begins with a header of 20 to 60 bytes. The fixed part is 20 bytes. The diagram shows the layout in 32-bit rows, which is also the way the specification and packet analysers present it.

blocks.text:
#### Time to live and the protocol field

The **TTL** field prevents a datagram from circulating forever when routing tables contain a loop. A host sets the initial value (commonly 64 on Linux and macOS, 128 on Windows; the exact default is configurable) and each router decrements it by one. When a router decrements a TTL to zero, it discards the datagram and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message to the source. The traceroute tool exploits exactly this behaviour (see the chapter on ICMP). Despite its name, TTL is a hop count, not a time.

The **protocol** field tells the receiving host which module handles the payload. The receiver demultiplexes on this value before the transport layer applies its own port-based demultiplexing.

blocks.text:
#### Fragmentation

Each link has a **maximum transmission unit** (MTU), the largest IP datagram it can carry. Ethernet uses 1500 bytes. When a router must forward a datagram larger than the MTU of the outgoing link, IPv4 permits the router to **fragment** it, unless the DF flag is set. Each fragment is an independent datagram with its own IP header. The rules are:

- Every fragment copies the identification, source, destination and protocol fields of the original.
- The fragment offset gives the position of the fragment's data within the original payload, divided by 8. Therefore every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 bytes of data.
- All fragments except the last have MF = 1. The last has MF = 0 and a non-zero offset.
- Routers never reassemble. Only the destination host reassembles, using the tuple (source, destination, protocol, identification) and a reassembly timer; if a fragment is missing when the timer expires, the whole datagram is discarded.

blocks.text:
Fragmentation is costly. A loss of any single fragment destroys the entire datagram, so the delivery probability falls from (1 - p) to (1 - p)^n for n fragments with independent loss probability p. Fragments also defeat stateless packet filters because only the first fragment contains the transport header with the port numbers. For these reasons modern stacks avoid fragmentation: TCP chooses a segment size that fits the path MTU, and Path MTU Discovery sets DF on every packet (see the chapter on ICMP). IPv6 removed router fragmentation altogether.

#### The header checksum

The header checksum protects the header against corruption in transit and in router memory. It is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of all 16-bit words of the header, computed with the checksum field set to zero (RFC 791 and the computation guide in RFC 1071). A receiver recomputes the sum over the complete header including the checksum field. A valid header yields 0xFFFF in the sum, that is, 0 after the final complement. The payload is not covered: TCP and UDP carry their own checksums. Because each router decrements the TTL, each router must also update the checksum. Implementations do this incrementally (RFC 1624) rather than summing the whole header again.

### Worked trace

blocks.text:
#### Checksum computation

The ten 16-bit words of the header, with the checksum field treated as 0x0000, are added with end-around carry.

blocks.caption: Step-by-step computation of the header checksum.

blocks.text:
The sum 0x2df53 has a carry out of the low 16 bits. Folding the carry gives 0xdf53 + 0x2 = 0xdf55. The one's complement of 0xdf55 is 0x20aa, which is the value placed in the checksum field. The receiver sums all ten words including 0x20aa: 0xdf55 + 0x20aa = 0xffff, and the complement is 0, so the header is accepted.

#### Effect of one router hop

The first router decrements TTL from 64 to 63. The word 0x4006 becomes 0x3f06, which is 0x0100 smaller. The old checksum no longer verifies, so the router adds 0x0100 to the checksum with end-around carry and writes 0x21aa. This value equals the checksum computed from scratch over the new header, as the program in the next section confirms.

#### Fragmentation of a 4000-byte datagram

An application sends a UDP datagram with 3972 bytes of data. With the 8-byte UDP header the IP payload is 3980 bytes and the total length is 4000. The outgoing link has an MTU of 1500, so the maximum data per fragment is 1500 - 20 = 1480 bytes, which is divisible by 8. The following table lists the three fragments (identification 0x3a7f, protocol 17).

The data bytes add up to 1480 + 1480 + 1020 = 3980. The offsets are 0 / 8 = 0, 1480 / 8 = 185 and 2960 / 8 = 370. The word 0x20b9 combines MF (0x2000) with offset 185 (0x00b9). The destination collects the three fragments, orders them by offset, concatenates their data and passes 3980 bytes to UDP once the fragment with MF = 0 and all bytes before it have arrived.

### Hands-on

The header checksum is simple enough to verify in a short Java program. The program builds the header of the worked trace in a `ByteBuffer`, computes the checksum, verifies it, and then repeats the computation after the TTL change of the first hop.

A server's view of the client address depends on the proxies in between. The next program starts a `com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer` on the loopback interface and reports both the address of the TCP peer and the `X-Forwarded-For` header, which load balancers use to carry the original client address.

The peer address is the immediate TCP neighbour. In a deployment behind a load balancer it is the balancer's address, and the original client address is available only in the forwarding header. blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The `X-Forwarded-For` header is supplied by the client unless a trusted proxy overwrites it. An application that uses its first value for access control or rate limiting can be bypassed by sending a forged header. Use the rightmost value appended by the trusted proxy, or the framework support that restricts accepted proxies.

### Questions to expect

1. **1. What is the difference between connectionless and connection-oriented delivery, and which does**

#### IP provide?

IP is connectionless: each datagram is forwarded independently with no setup and no per-flow state in routers. Connection-oriented delivery (TCP) maintains state at the endpoints for sequencing, acknowledgement and flow control. IP provides only best-effort delivery.

#### 2. Why does the IPv4 header contain a checksum that covers only the header?

Routers must verify and update the header at every hop, so a cheap header-only checksum keeps forwarding fast. Payload integrity is the responsibility of TCP and UDP, which carry end-to-end checksums. IPv6 dropped the header checksum entirely, because link layers and transport protocols already verify integrity.

#### 3. What does a router do to the header of a forwarded packet?

It decrements the TTL, discards the packet and signals ICMP Time Exceeded if the TTL reaches zero, updates the header checksum and, if necessary, fragments the packet. The link-layer frame is rebuilt completely with new source and destination MAC addresses; the IP addresses stay unchanged unless NAT is applied.

#### 4. Why must the fragment offset be a multiple of 8 bytes?

The offset field has 13 bits but the datagram can be 65,535 bytes long, so the offset counts units of 8 bytes. Every fragment except the last must therefore carry a multiple of 8 data bytes.

1. **5. A 4000-byte datagram crosses an MTU of 1500. How many fragments result and what are their**

#### offsets?

The data per fragment is 1480 bytes (1500 minus the 20-byte header). The payload of 3980 bytes needs three fragments carrying 1480, 1480 and 1020 bytes, with offsets 0, 185 and 370 and MF values 1, 1 and 0.

#### 6. Who reassembles fragments and why not the routers?

The destination host. Fragments can take different paths, so a router cannot be sure that it sees all of them, and reassembly would require buffering and state in every router.

#### 7. What is the purpose of the TTL field, and is it measured in seconds?

It bounds the lifetime of a datagram so that routing loops do not cause permanent circulation. It is a hop count: each router subtracts one, regardless of the time spent.

#### 8. How does a server behind a load balancer learn the client address?

From the `X-Forwarded-For` or `Forwarded` header set by an HTTP load balancer, or from the PROXY protocol for TCP balancers. The socket peer address is the balancer. The header must be trusted only from known proxies.

#### 9. What is the maximum size of an IPv4 datagram and what limits it?

65,535 bytes, because the total length field has 16 bits. In practice datagrams stay near the link MTU, typically 1500 bytes.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Follow-up chain: why does TCP rarely cause IP fragmentation? TCP advertises a maximum segment size (MSS) during the handshake, derived from the interface MTU (1460 for an MTU of 1500 with 20-byte IP and TCP headers). The sender never builds a segment larger than the smaller of the two MSS values and usually sets DF, so oversized packets are detected through ICMP instead of being fragmented. UDP applications have no such mechanism and must size their datagrams themselves.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- IP is connectionless and best effort; reliability belongs to TCP or the application.
- The 20-byte header carries addresses, TTL, protocol, fragmentation fields and a header-only checksum that every router recomputes.
- Fragment offsets are counted in 8-byte units; only the destination reassembles, and one lost fragment loses the datagram.
- TTL is a hop count that stops routing loops and powers traceroute.
- Behind proxies the socket peer address is the proxy; the client address travels in forwarding headers that must be trusted selectively.

Allocating address space in blocks of 256, 65,536 or 16.7 million addresses forced organisations to request far more space than they needed, and it filled the global routing table with thousands of small entries. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR, RFC 4632) removed the fixed boundaries. A network is described by an address and a **prefix length** of any value from 0 to 32, and routers aggregate adjacent blocks into a single advertisement. Subnetting, which divides one block into smaller blocks, and summarisation, which combines blocks, are the two operations that every network engineer and every cloud architect performs. Both reduce to bit arithmetic.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Prefix length and subnet mask

The notation `192.168.10.0/26` states that the first 26 bits are the network prefix and the remaining 6 bits identify hosts. The equivalent **subnet mask** has ones in the prefix positions and zeros in the host positions: 26 ones give `11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000`, which is `255.255.255.192`. A device decides whether a destination is on its own network with one operation: if (destination AND mask) equals (own address AND mask), the destination is local and is reached by ARP on the link; otherwise the packet goes to the default gateway.

The four values that describe a subnet are derived as follows.

- **Network address**: address AND mask (all host bits zero). It names the subnet and is not assigned to a host.
- **Broadcast address**: the network address with all host bits set to one. A datagram sent to it reaches every host in the subnet.
- **Usable host range**: from network + 1 to broadcast - 1.
- **Number of usable hosts**: 2^h - 2 for h host bits. Two point-to-point exceptions exist: a /31 has two usable addresses (RFC 3021) and a /32 identifies exactly one interface, as used for loopback addresses and host routes.

blocks.caption: The address 192.168.10.77 with mask /26 written bit by bit: the AND operation clears the six host bits and produces the network 192.168.10.64; setting them to ones produces the broadcast address 192.168.10.127.

blocks.text: A shortcut avoids binary conversion. In the octet where the mask is not 0 or 255, the **block size** is 256 minus the mask value in that octet. For 255.255.255.192 the block size is 64, so the subnets in the last octet start at 0, 64, 128 and 192. An address belongs to the block whose start is the largest multiple of the block size not exceeding the address octet: 77 lies in the block starting at 64.

blocks.caption: Subnet quick reference for the last octet (the first three octets are 255).

blocks.text:
#### Subnetting into equal parts

To split a block into N equal subnets, borrow b bits from the host part, where 2^b is at least N. The prefix grows by b, each subnet has 2^(h - b) addresses, and the subnet identifiers appear in the borrowed bits. For `192.168.10.0/24` and N = 4, b = 2 and the new prefix is /26.

#### Variable-length subnet masks

Equal subnets waste addresses when the segments differ in size. **Variable-length subnet masking** (VLSM) allocates a block of the smallest sufficient size to each segment. The procedure has four steps.

1. For each segment, find the smallest h such that 2^h - 2 is at least the required number of hosts; the prefix is 32 - h.
2. Sort the segments by size, largest first.
3. Assign blocks consecutively from the start of the parent block. Sorting guarantees that every block begins at an address that is a multiple of its own size (alignment); an unaligned block cannot be expressed as a single prefix.
4. Check that the total fits in the parent block and record the unused remainder for growth.

#### Summarisation (supernetting)

A router that receives routes to several adjacent subnets can advertise one shorter prefix, provided the blocks are contiguous, the count is a power of two and the first block is aligned to the size of the combined block. Summarisation shrinks routing tables and hides internal changes from the rest of the network. The method is to find the longest common bit prefix of all networks.

blocks.text:
Private ranges are the reason that NAT exists (see the chapter on NAT and DHCP). Because every organisation uses the same few ranges, two networks that must be connected, for example through a VPN or VPC peering, cannot overlap. Overlap is one of the most frequent avoidable mistakes in cloud and container networking.

### Worked trace

#### Example 1: classify an address and find its boundaries

Given 192.168.10.77/26 (the diagram above), the mask octet is 192, the block size is 256 - 192 = 64 and 77 lies in the block starting at 64. The network is 192.168.10.64, the broadcast is 64 + 63 = 127, the usable range is .65 to .126 (62 hosts). The second example in the program output below uses a larger prefix: 172.16.5.130/20 has a mask of 255.255.240.0, a block size of 16 in the third octet and 5 lies in the block starting at 0, so the network is 172.16.0.0 and the broadcast is 172.16.15.255.

#### Example 2: equal subnets

Requirement: six departments, at most 25 hosts each, from 192.168.20.0/24. Six subnets need b = 3 bits (2^3 = 8 is at least 6) and leave 5 host bits, which give 30 usable hosts, sufficient for 25. The prefix is /27 and the subnets are 192.168.20.0, .32, .64, .96, .128, .160, .192 and .224 (eight subnets, two spare).

#### Example 3: VLSM design

Requirement: from `192.168.50.0/24` allocate LAN-A (100 hosts), LAN-B (50), LAN-C (25), LAN-D (10) and two point-to-point router links (2 hosts each).

#### Example 4: summarisation

Four branch offices use 192.168.0.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24 and 192.168.3.0/24. The third octets are 00000000, 00000001, 00000010 and 00000011, so the first six bits agree. The summary is 192.168.0.0/22 with mask 255.255.252.0. Three of the four networks (0, 1 and 2) cannot be expressed as one prefix: the best aggregation is 192.168.0.0/23 plus 192.168.2.0/24, which the Python `ipaddress` module also reports for these inputs.

### Hands-on

The listing implements a small subnet calculator with `long` arithmetic. `describe` prints the derived values of one CIDR block and `vlsm` assigns blocks to a list of host requirements, largest first.

What to notice: the `vlsm` method finds the smallest bit count with `(1L << bits) - 2 >= hosts`, advances the cursor by the block size, and therefore reproduces the table of Example 3. The 32-bit values are held in a `long` so that masks and addresses stay positive and do not sign-extend when shifted.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A prefix of /31 or /32 has no network and broadcast address in the usual sense. Calculators that apply the 2^h - 2 rule produce -1 hosts or 0 hosts for these prefixes. The program above applies the exception explicitly.

### Questions to expect

#### 1. Given 10.20.30.40/21, what are the network, broadcast and host range?

The mask is 255.255.248.0, the block size in the third octet is 8, and 30 lies in the block starting at 24. The network is 10.20.24.0, the broadcast 10.20.31.255, and the hosts are 10.20.24.1 to 10.20.31.254 (2046 hosts).

#### 2. How many usable hosts does a /27 provide and why minus two?

32 - 27 = 5 host bits give 32 addresses. The all-zero host part names the network and the all-ones host part is the directed broadcast, so 30 addresses remain for interfaces.

1. **3. Split 192.168.1.0/24 into at least 10 subnets. What is the new mask and the hosts per subnet?**

Four borrowed bits give 16 subnets (three give only 8). The prefix is /28, the mask 255.255.255.240, and each subnet has 14 usable hosts.

#### 4. What is VLSM and why is the largest-first order important?

VLSM assigns each segment a prefix that fits its size. Placing large blocks first keeps every block aligned on a multiple of its own size, so no address space is lost to alignment gaps and every block is a valid prefix.

#### 5. When can routes be summarised?

When the networks are contiguous, their number is a power of two and the first network address is aligned to the size of the combined block. For example 192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.3.0/24 summarise to 192.168.0.0/22, whereas 192.168.1.0/24 through 192.168.4.0/24 do not.

#### 6. Why can two hosts in the same subnet communicate without a router?

The sender finds the destination inside its own prefix by the AND test and resolves the destination MAC address with ARP on the local link. A router is involved only when the prefix test fails.

#### 7. What is the difference between a private address and a link-local address?

A private address (RFC 1918) is routable inside an organisation and assigned by an administrator or DHCP. A link-local address (169.254.0.0/16 in IPv4, fe80::/10 in IPv6) is valid only on the attached link and is never forwarded by routers.

#### 8. Why is 100.64.0.0/10 not part of RFC 1918?

It is shared address space reserved for carrier-grade NAT (RFC 6598). Using a separate block prevents a service provider from clashing with the private ranges customers already use inside their homes and offices.

#### 9. How would the choice of address ranges affect a VPN between two offices?

Both offices must use non-overlapping ranges. If both use 192.168.1.0/24, a route to that prefix is ambiguous and traffic cannot be directed to the remote side without translation or renumbering.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Follow-up: a /24 host sends to a destination whose address ANDed with the mask equals its own network. What happens next? The destination is on-link. The host does not use the gateway. It broadcasts an ARP request for the destination address, caches the reply and sends the frame directly to that MAC address. If the destination is not on-link, the host resolves the MAC address of the default gateway instead, and the IP destination address remains the original destination.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A prefix length splits an address into network and host bits; network = address AND mask, broadcast = host bits all ones, usable hosts = 2^h - 2.
- Equal subnetting borrows b bits for 2^b subnets; VLSM sizes each block to its segment, largest first, to keep blocks aligned.
- Summarisation replaces contiguous aligned blocks with the shared bit prefix, for example four /24 networks with a /22.
- Private (RFC 1918), shared (100.64.0.0/10), loopback, link-local and documentation ranges are not globally routable; overlapping private ranges are a common integration fault.
- The same AND test decides on-link delivery versus use of the default gateway.
